questions.stem: A learner encounters this problem. Using the adjacency lists 0:[1,2], 1:[0,2,3], 2:[0,1,4], 3:[1,4,5], 4:[2,3,5], 5:[3,4] with neighbors visited in increasing order, which sequence is the depth-first traversal from vertex 5?

options.misconception: rotates the start vertex to the end
uses breadth-first search instead
reverses the discovery order

questions.explanation: DFS uses a stack (or recursion) and follows a path as deep as possible before backtracking. Starting at 5, the visit order is 5 -> 3 -> 1 -> 0 -> 2 -> 4; the other option is the opposite traversal strategy.
questions.hint: Go as deep as possible along the smallest neighbor first, then backtrack.

questions.stem: The item below needs a solution. In the unweighted connected graph 0:[1,2], 1:[0,2,3], 2:[0,1,4], 3:[1,4,5], 4:[2,3,5], 5:[3,4], how many edges are on a shortest path from vertex 3 to vertex 3?

options.misconception: counts vertices on the path instead of edges
assumes an unreachable target when the graph is connected
off by one in the level count

questions.explanation: In an unweighted graph a BFS from 3 discovers 3 at level 0, which is the number of edges on the shortest path. A path with 0 edges has 1 vertices, which is why counting vertices is the frequent slip.

questions.stem: Trace the process described below. Using Kruskal's algorithm on the weighted edges [0-1:4, 0-2:2, 1-2:1, 1-3:5, 2-3:8, 2-4:10, 3-4:2, 3-5:6, 4-5:3], what is the total weight of a minimum spanning tree?

options.misconception: takes the five cheapest edges without skipping cycles
adds every edge weight instead of selecting the spanning tree
adds one extra edge weight

questions.explanation: Sorting edges by weight and accepting an edge only when it joins two different components gives a spanning tree of total weight 13. Adding every edge, or the five cheapest without cycle checks, overshoots because it keeps redundant edges.

questions.stem: Analyze this concrete example. After one pass of bubble sort on the array 2, 7, 8, 1, 3, 6, 5, what is the array state?

options.misconception: assumes a single pass fully sorts the whole array
applies the wrong rearrangement for this pass
leaves the array unchanged as if no pass occurred

questions.explanation: One pass of bubble sort moves only the element being placed in that pass; the prefix it touches becomes ordered but the rest stays as before, yielding 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, 5, 8. Thinking the whole array is sorted after one pass is a common misconception.
questions.hint: Simulate exactly one outer-loop iteration, not the entire sort.

questions.stem: Consider the following question. Which sort uses O(1) auxiliary space and is in-place with O(n log n) average time?

counting sort is not comparison-based and uses O(k) space

returns the previous Fibonacci number by stopping one step early
advances the recurrence by one index too far

takes only the single largest value
adds every house and ignores the adjacency constraint

adds one from an inclusive diagonal index

questions.stem: Derive the result from the facts. Which property must hold for a greedy algorithm to be provably optimal?

input size monotonicity is not a standard correctness condition
a large search space does not justify greedy correctness

adds one from miscounting the initial number of components

questions.stem: Read the setup and derive the answer. A Bloom filter has m = 13 bits and hash functions h1(x)=x mod m, h2(x)=(2x+1) mod m. Which bit positions are set when key 3 is inserted?

swaps the two hash formulas
uses k+1 style hashes instead of the defined h1 and h2

assumes direct addressing without any traversal

questions.stem: Study the setup and answer it. For a sorted array of n = 255 elements, how many key comparisons does binary search make in the worst case?

doubles the depth instead of recognizing that each step halves the interval
off by one above the depth by counting the empty final interval

questions.stem: Solve using the information shown. A dynamic array starts with capacity 2 and doubles its capacity whenever it is full. After 11 append operations, how many element copies have occurred in total?

options.misconception: assumes exactly one resize of the initial capacity occurs
counts only the m insertions and ignores every resize copy
overestimates by imagining a copy on every append

questions.explanation: Resizes happen when size reaches capacity; the copied amounts are 2, 4, and so on up to the last resize, summing to 14. Because each element is copied at most once per doubling level, the total is below 2m, giving amortized O(1) per append.
questions.hint: Track size and capacity together; a resize copies the current size, then capacity doubles.

questions.stem: Compute the result for this case. For an input of size n = 6373, what is the worst-case auxiliary space (excluding the input) used by a single iterative loop over the input?

options.misconception: counts one stack frame or buffer slot per input element
mixes the time bound of a sort into its space bound
confuses the depth of a balanced recursion with a linear stack

questions.explanation: Auxiliary space counts extra memory beyond the input. For a single iterative loop over the input the dominant extra allocation grows as O(1); call-stack frames or a temporary buffer scale with that quantity, and this measure is distinct from the algorithm's running time.
